title: GNSS and the Lever Arm: Latitude and Longitude to Metres, and an Antenna That Is Not Where the Robot Is

questions.question: Why is a degree of longitude shorter than a degree of latitude?
options: The earth is wider at the equator
The meridians meet at the poles, so it is shorter by the cosine of the latitude
It is not, on a sphere
questions.explanation: A degree of latitude is the same length everywhere. A degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles: at 52 degrees north it is 68458 m, 38 percent less.

questions.question: One degree of latitude was:
questions.explanation: The earth's radius of 6371 km times one degree in radians. It is the same at every latitude.

questions.question: At 10 km the flat map was how far from the great circle?
questions.explanation: The flat map's error grows with distance: 0.036 m at 1 km, 3.55 m at 10 km, 357 m at 100 km. One origin serves a field, not a country.

questions.question: A robot turning on the spot with an antenna 0.5 m from its centre had an antenna moving at:
options: 0 m/s: the robot did not move
questions.explanation: The antenna goes round a circle of radius 0.5 m at 1 rad/s. A filter that takes it for the robot sees a robot moving at half a metre a second.

questions.question: With the heading wrong by 5 degrees, what was left after the lever correction?
options: 0.044 m, the lever times the error
questions.explanation: The lever is turned by the heading to subtract it. Five degrees is 0.087 rad, and 0.5 m times that is 0.044 m.

questions.question: Why should the antenna be as near the reference point as the sky allows?
options: The error of the correction is the lever times the heading error
The antenna sees more sky when low
A short lever needs no correction at all
questions.explanation: The lever still has to be subtracted. What shrinks with it is how much a heading error can spoil that subtraction.
